const DESIGN_AUTHORITY_EN = "## Design Authority and Consistency Principle v1

1. Resolve the design authority first. Read the current project's and target subproject's system variable `design.authority`, together with the authority repository, production documentation, and build and deployment bindings declared in the same configuration. Each project and subproject must resolve to its own effective authority; inherited values must identify their source. Resolve missing or conflicting bindings before design work, without guessing from directory placement, the parent project, or memory.
2. Inspect existing components and standards. Use the authority's published contract to identify component families, variants, states, layouts, and interactions before implementation. Reuse existing capabilities and include missing ones in the authority's change scope.
3. Change the authority first. Every addition or change to a component, visual design, or design standard starts with a PR to the authority repository, covering implementation, standards, working examples, and applicable validation. Do not create a separate design in the application and document it afterwards.
4. Consume changes after production succeeds. The application may use the new capability only after the authority PR is merged, its declared production documentation or component library is published successfully, and its declared build and deployment service succeeds, with all evidence bound to the same source commit or artifact version. A local pass, preview deployment, or reachable page does not establish production success. Include this dependency when organizing the batch and do not consume the change before it is satisfied.
5. Keep component families consistent. Preserve the family's colors, typography, spacing, sizing, radii, borders, icons, motion, and interaction states. Added features follow existing selection, feedback, and keyboard patterns. Compare equivalent components directly to prevent a substantially different visual or interaction language; obtain explicit Owner agreement before a substantial style change. Adding a substantially divergent implementation to the authority does not establish family consistency or Owner visual acceptance. Check every added or changed component and variant: equivalent tasks use equivalent controls, with consistent meanings and expectations for selection, navigation, saving, undoing, resetting, error feedback, and keyboard interaction.
6. Consume the published contract. Use published components, tokens, or an authority-approved static consumption method, bind the actual version, and refresh generated contracts and stylesheet snapshots together. Do not copy documentation-only styles, recreate reusable components in the application, or conceal missing authority support with local overrides.

When the application already uses a component, variant, or design standard absent from the authority or its production release, identify the consumer locations and missing evidence. Complete the same authority PR, production publication, and build sequence before continuing affected application changes. Record machine verification and Owner visual acceptance separately.
8. Separate rules from values. Reference system variables and their authority contracts in the rule body instead of hard-coding project names, repository addresses, documentation URLs, deployment vendors, versions, or component measurements. Store actual values in project or subproject configuration. Mark unavailable configuration capabilities or unreadable evidence as unconfigured or unverified. Use the current task's existing authorization for commits and publication.

Once decomposition is done, group the Subtasks into packages first: Subtasks that depend on one another or change the same files go into the same package and are done in order within it; Subtasks that do not affect one another each form a package of their own. The concurrency limit is execution.maxConcurrentSubagents; when that value exceeds the host's limit or is not set, dispatch by the host's rules.
